name: The Watson Beech

location.address: 1875 SW Park Ave (PSU Millar Library entrance)

verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 238, Heritage Tree #54)

Portland Parks & Recreation Urban Forestry, 'From Stumptown to Treetown: A Field Guide for Interpreting Portland's History through its Heritage Trees' by David-Paul B. Hedberg, https://www.portland.gov/trees/documents/stumptown-treetown/download, Stop 1
access: Free, always open. Stands on the open lawn at the main entrance to PSU's Millar Library, a public university campus walkway.
transport: Downtown Portland, on the PSU campus; MAX Blue/Red/Green Line and Portland Streetcar both stop within a couple of minutes' walk (Transit Mall / Kings Hill-SW Salmon station area).
verify_notes: Register: Copper Beech, Heritage Tree #54, listed 1995, planted c.1890, height 84ft/25.6m, diameter 72in/182.9cm, circumference 18.75ft/5.71m (register units are feet/inches, converted here). Second source (Stumptown to Treetown field guide, official PP&R Urban Forestry publication) independently corroborates species, planting date and location, and adds the story: planted around 1890 by ironworks/shipbuilding merchant Frank Watson (or his wife Mary Whalley Watson) beside their new home on the corner of Hall and Park; the house was demolished in 1965-68 when Portland State College built its library (architects Skidmore, Owings & Merrill), and for reasons no source records, PSU chose to save the beech rather than clear it, so it became the literal centerpiece of the library's front lawn instead. What it witnessed: the transformation of a Victorian residential corner into the PSU campus, and decades of students using the lawn beneath it (a 1975 photo shows a crowd gathered on the grass under the tree). No disagreement between sources. Alive: both sources describe it as a standing, thriving campus landmark; no removal or hazard notice found.

name: The Farrell Planetree

location.address: NW corner of SW Park Ave & SW Main St

verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 441, Heritage Tree #2)
Portland Parks & Recreation Urban Forestry, 'From Stumptown to Treetown' field guide, https://www.portland.gov/trees/documents/stumptown-treetown/download, Stop 3
access: Free, always open. Standing in the street planting strip at a downtown corner, fully public.
transport: Downtown Portland; MAX Blue/Red/Green Line and Portland Streetcar both stop within a few minutes' walk of the Park Blocks.
verify_notes: Register: London planetree (register spells it 'London planetree'; house style is London Plane), Heritage Tree #2, listed 1973 (one of the very first Heritage Trees designated, the register's own tree #2), planted c.1880, height 63ft/19.2m, diameter 54in/137.2cm, circumference 14.3ft/4.36m. Second source (Stumptown to Treetown) gives the origin story: planted by Sylvester Farrell, a feed-and-grocery merchant turned salmon canner and Portland City Councilman, beside his family home on this corner; allegedly a gift from U.S. Senator J.N. Dolph. An 1880 photo shows it as a young sapling next to the Farrell house, which was later demolished for what is now a parking lot; the tree outlived the house by well over a century. The guide notes the species is 'erroneously called a Sycamore' locally, and that the tree was protected as a Portland Historic Landmark in 1973 before formally becoming Heritage Tree #2. What it witnessed: Portland's shift from 'Stumptown' (cleared of its native forest) to a city that deliberately replanted itself, and the site's own change from a private Victorian home to a parking lot. No disagreement between sources; both alive-status sources (register plus field guide, itself citing City of Portland Urban Forestry heritage tree files) describe an actively maintained downtown Heritage Tree.

name: The Kamm Walnut

location.address: 1600 SW Salmon St (Lincoln High School, corner of SW Salmon & SW 14th Ave)

verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 353, Heritage Tree #35)
Portland Parks & Recreation Urban Forestry, 'From Stumptown to Treetown' field guide, https://www.portland.gov/trees/documents/stumptown-treetown/download, Stop 5
access: Visible and reachable from the public sidewalk at the SW Salmon/SW 14th corner (register ownership: Portland Public Schools, standing at the edge of the Lincoln High School grounds). Stand at the street corner rather than crossing onto school property, especially during school hours.
transport: Goose Hollow, a short walk west of downtown; Portland Streetcar and MAX both have stops within about 10 minutes' walk (Goose Hollow/SW Jefferson MAX station is closest).
verify_notes: Register: Black Walnut, Heritage Tree #35, listed 1994, plaque metadata 'PLANTED C. 1880s', height 95ft/29.0m, diameter 53in/134.6cm, circumference 13.9ft/4.24m. DISAGREEMENT, flagged: the field guide's own narrative text dates the planting to 'around 1871, when this tree was planted on the north corner of the newly constructed home of Jacob Kamm', roughly a decade earlier than the guide's own plaque-derived header ('PLANTED C. 1880s'); age range given here (140-155 years) spans both. Second source (Stumptown to Treetown) supplies the story: this walnut is the last living remnant of the 14-acre estate of Jacob Kamm, a Swiss immigrant steamship engineer who made his fortune in Columbia River shipping (Oregon Steam and Navigation Company) and built a French Second Empire mansion here; his wife Caroline Agusta Gray had grown up among the first missionary families with the Nez Perce in Idaho. The Kamms sold the property in 1910 for Lincoln High School; when the current school building went up in 1952, architect Hollis Johnston deliberately kept the walnut and its neighbours in his site design. What it witnessed: the site's transformation from countryside estate at the literal edge of 1870s Portland, through the construction of Lincoln High, to today's I-405 freeway frontage. Known locally enough that the guide notes 'Ask a graduate of Lincoln High School about this large Black Walnut and you'll likely get a story.' No dead/removal signal found in either source.

name: The Miller Pine
verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 101, Heritage Tree listed 1993)
Portland Parks & Recreation Urban Forestry, 'From Stumptown to Treetown' field guide, https://www.portland.gov/trees/documents/stumptown-treetown/download, Stop 6
access: Free, always open. Standing in a built-out street planter at a Goose Hollow intersection (register ownership: Right Of Way / TriMet), fully public.
transport: Goose Hollow; the MAX Blue/Red Line Goose Hollow/SW Jefferson St station is a short walk away.
verify_notes: Register: Austrian Pine, listed 1993, planted c.1870s, height 102ft/31.1m, diameter 39in/99.1cm, circumference 10.6ft/3.23m. Register note: 'believed to have been planted sometime in the late 19th century by Henry Miller, one of Portland's first florists.' Second source (Stumptown to Treetown, Stop 6, 'Henry Miller's Nursery') independently confirms both the attribution and the site history: this stretch of Goose Hollow was, in the 1870s-1890s, well outside the city limits and the location of Miller's plant nursery, seed farm and floral supply business; the tree stands with a large Cedar of Lebanon nearby, both apparently imported and planted on Miller's nursery grounds. A 1959 photo of the Jacob Kamm House (see The Kamm Walnut, por_004, a few blocks away) shows this pine and the cedar already mature in the background. What it witnessed: the conversion of a semi-rural nursery district into today's dense Goose Hollow neighbourhood beside I-405. No disagreement between sources on species, era or location.

name: The Rockey Elm
verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 349, Heritage Tree #46)
Portland Parks & Recreation Urban Forestry, 'From Stumptown to Treetown' field guide, https://www.portland.gov/trees/documents/stumptown-treetown/download, Stop 8
access: Free, always open. Standing in the sidewalk planting strip on NW Flanders St, fully public.
transport: Northwest District (Nob Hill area); Portland Streetcar NS Line stops a few blocks south on NW Northrup/Lovejoy; roughly a 10-15 minute walk from the NW 21st/23rd Ave shopping streets.
verify_notes: Register: Dutch Elm, Heritage Tree #46, listed 1995, planted c.1900, height 80ft/24.4m, diameter 58in/147.3cm, circumference 15.1ft/4.60m. Register note: 'condemned to be cut down by the Portland City Council in 1963, but a devoted group of tree lovers saved its life.' Second source (Stumptown to Treetown, Stop 8, 'Natural and Human Obstacles') gives the full account: the tree first survived the Columbus Day Storm of 1962 (a category-3-strength windstorm, 116mph gusts recorded in Portland), then a year later the property owner in front of the planting strip sought a permit to remove it over fears of root damage to his building. Neighbourhood architect Lewis Crucher parked his car beside the tree to physically block a removal crew; Mayor Terry Schrunk placed a moratorium on the cutting permit pending city forester and engineer reports; Dr Eugene W. Rockey wrote to the Oregonian recalling that his father planted the tree in 1900 in front of their newly built home, complete with a wooden slat guard to keep the family's buggy horse from nipping the sapling. The saga ran in the Oregonian for months, including a public memorial-style vigil and a published poem; the city forester and parks superintendent ultimately found the tree safe and healthy and denied the removal permit. Stands directly across NW Flanders St from The Storm Elm (por_007), and the guide treats the pair as one stop ('the two Elms'). No disagreement between sources; both describe the tree as a preserved, actively protected Heritage Tree.

Portland Parks & Recreation Urban Forestry, 'From Stumptown to Treetown' field guide, https://www.portland.gov/trees/documents/stumptown-treetown/download, Stop 8
access: Free, always open. Standing in the sidewalk planting strip on NW Flanders St, fully public.
transport: Northwest District (Nob Hill area); Portland Streetcar NS Line stops a few blocks south on NW Northrup/Lovejoy; roughly a 10-15 minute walk from the NW 21st/23rd Ave shopping streets.
verify_notes: Register: English Elm, Heritage Tree #36, listed 1994, planted 1902-1903, height 80ft/24.4m, diameter 54in/137.2cm, circumference 14.1ft/4.30m. Register note: 'the only elm left standing on the north side of that block on Flanders after the Columbus Day storm of 1962.' Second source (Stumptown to Treetown, Stop 8) corroborates and adds context: this and The Rockey Elm (por_006, directly across the street) both survived the 1962 storm that felled roughly 15 billion board feet of Pacific Northwest timber; the guide notes it is no small feat that these two specific trees came through it. A smaller elm nearby on the same block was later removed after succumbing to Dutch Elm Disease (spread by the elm bark beetle, introduced from Asia via Europe); the city and volunteers now inoculate remaining elms against the disease. No disagreement between sources on species, survival story or location; treated by the guide as one paired stop with por_006.

name: The Balch Creek Fir

location.address: Lower Macleay Park / Balch Creek spur trail, near NW Cornell Rd, Forest Park

verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 211)
PSU Vanguard, 'Experience Portland's most historic trees', https://psuvanguard.com/experience-portlands-most-historic-trees/
access: Free, always open. Standing on Portland Parks & Recreation land inside Forest Park/Macleay Park, on the Lower Macleay spur trail about 100 yards from the stone house ('Witch's Castle') ruin along Balch Creek. Reached on foot via a public park trail, not roadside.
transport: Access via the Lower Macleay trailhead, 2960 NW Upshur St; TriMet bus lines 15, 26 and 77 stop within a few blocks (NW Thurman/27th-29th or NW Vaughn/27th), then it is roughly a 15-20 minute walk up the Lower Macleay/Wildwood Trail along Balch Creek to reach the tree.
verify_notes: Register: Douglas Fir, height 243ft/74.1m, diameter 70in/177.8cm, circumference 18.3ft/5.58m. Register note: 'the largest Douglas-fir in Portland... found 100 yards from the stone house on the Lower Macleay spur trail along Balch Creek.' Second source (PSU Vanguard student newspaper, a piece specifically on Portland's historic trees) independently states it is 'the tallest tree in the City of Portland at 243 feet in height with a girth of 18.3 feet' and that 'a large stone by the side of the trail marks a Portland Heritage Tree' at this spot, matching the register's height and girth figures exactly and confirming the trailside marker. What it is remarkable for: simply the tallest tree in Portland, a native Douglas Fir standing in the steep, shaded Balch Creek ravine that makes up the lower end of Forest Park, one of the largest urban forest reserves in the US. name: The Hoyt Dawn Redwood

location.address: Hoyt Arboretum, near SW Bray Ln, 4000 SW Fairview Blvd

verified_sources: data/registers/portland-heritage-trees.json (City of Portland Heritage Tree register, CC BY-SA, objectid 163)
Travel Oregon (official state tourism site), 'Dawn Redwood - Heritage Tree', https://traveloregon.com/things-to-do/culture-history/historic-sites-oregon-trail/dawn-redwood-heritage-tree/
Hoyt Arboretum's own site, https://www.hoytarboretum.org/majestic-redwoods-at-hoyt-arboretum/ and https://www.portland.gov/trees/metasequoia-glyptostroboides
access: Free, always open, no admission charge. Hoyt Arboretum is a public Portland Parks & Recreation arboretum within Washington Park.
transport: MAX Blue/Red Line Washington Park station (the deepest transit station in North America) is about a half-mile walk along the Overlook Trail to the Arboretum Visitor Center, or take the seasonal free Washington Park shuttle from the station to the Hoyt Arboretum stop.
verify_notes: Register: Dawn Redwood, height 103ft/31.4m, diameter 41in/104.1cm, circumference 10.8ft/3.29m. Register note: 'This tree is an Oregon Heritage Tree. It was the first Dawn Redwood to bear cones in the Western hemisphere in 8 million years.' Two independent sources (Travel Oregon, Hoyt Arboretum's own site) both instead say 'about 6 million years', not 8: 'this tree became the first in the Western hemisphere to produce cones in about 6 million years' (1952). FLAGGED, genuine disagreement on the headline number, not resolved; deliver both figures rather than pick a winner. All sources agree on the underlying story: Metasequoia was known only from fossils and presumed extinct until a living stand was found in a remote Chinese valley in 1944; Harvard's Arnold Arboretum organised an international seed-collecting expedition in 1947, Hoyt Arboretum was among the US recipients and planted its seedlings in 1948, and this tree bore the first cones of any Metasequoia grown in the Western hemisphere since the species' rediscovery, in 1952. Age estimate (75-80 years) is based on the well-corroborated 1948 planting year. What it witnessed: living proof of a species assumed extinct for millions of years reproducing again outside China for the first time. No removal or death signal found; both later sources describe it in the present tense as a standing, celebrated feature of the Arboretum's redwood collection.
